building.label: Office tower
building.why_chosen: Sharpest demand-charge exposure on the site: p99/median = 2.9, weekday peak at 14:00, night/day = 0.44. All-electric cooling (corr with outdoor temp = 0.54, 1.85x lift from mild to hot days). 13,759 sqm.

tariff.order_ref: TNERC Tariff Order T.P. No. 1 of 2023 as amended for FY 2025-26; ToD windows per Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Amendment Rules 2023

scenarios.label: Normal month
scenarios.description: June 2017 as it actually happened, no injected failure.

scenarios.label: Heatwave
scenarios.description: Outdoor temperature +6 °C and base load +25% for three days, beyond anything in the forecaster's training window.

scenarios.label: Sensor dropout
scenarios.description: The forecast input freezes for two hours. The controller keeps acting on its last good estimate, which is what happens when a BMS point dies.

scenarios.label: Grid outage
scenarios.description: Grid import forced to zero for two hours; only critical load is served. The controller must ride through on thermal mass.

runs.blurb: A deadband thermostat at a fixed 24 °C setpoint, water heater always hot, EVs charging flat out on arrival. Price-blind and peak-blind: what an uninstrumented building does today.
Tariff-aware but risk-blind: pre-cools ahead of the peak window, throttles through it, pushes deferrable load into cheap hours. No optimisation, no forecast.
The same MILP as ours, planning the demand ceiling on the *median* forecast instead of the 95th percentile. The only line of difference.
Substitutes base-load q95 and solar q05 into the demand-ceiling constraint. A chance constraint by quantile substitution.
Ours, but handed the true future base load. Still limited to a 16-hour rolling horizon, so it is not the achievable bound.
One MILP over the entire billing month with perfect foresight. The genuine upper bound, and the denominator for '% of oracle savings'.
